The post Prolific Hive and Nefilim ransomware affiliate sentenced to 70 months in prison appeared first on CyberScoop . A 36-year-old Ukrainian national was sentenced to 70 months in prison for participating in a string of ransomware attacks targeting various critical infrastructure operators and businesses from the middle of 2018 to late 2021, the Justice Department said Tuesday. Artem Aleksandrovych Stryzhak was involved in ransomware attacks on hospitals that disrupted patient care, government entities, a dentist office, a company in the oil and gas transportation industry and law firms. recent_posts.text: Open-source maintainers are so overwhelmed by AI-generated security reports that some have stopped accepting them. OpenAI’s Daybreak lead says the fix is higher-quality findings and far more coordination. The post Before you file that AI bug report, OpenAI has some advice appeared first on CyberScoop . Even OpenAI is admitting there is a lot of AI slop in the security space. An executive for the frontier AI company said Tuesday that AI -generated vulnerability reports are overwhelming open-source maintainers, leading some to stop accepting submissions as the workload exceeds their capacity to review them. Michael Aiello, OpenAI’s cyber executive in residence, described the problem during a question-and-answer session Tuesday at the DataTribe Challenge in Washington, D.C., when he was asked how he viewed OpenAI ’s Patch the Planet program versus open-source maintainers banning AI-based submissions because of concerns about quality and clarity. “It’s an ecosystem problem where that [maintainer] is just not going to respond to hundreds and hundreds of AI-submitted vulnerabilities,” Aiello said. recent_posts.title: Smashing Security podcast #490: How Jared Kushner’s iPhone was allegedly hacked twice
recent_posts.text: Dutch spies, Russian hackers and Jared Kushner’s iPhone. It sounds like the ingredients for a thriller, but according to claims in a new book the US President's son-in-law may have been hacked twice. Is any of it true, and what does it tell us about the phones in our pockets? Meanwhile, James Ball explains that of the internet’s most trusted security keys were protected by numbers so small that one of them was... four. Yes, "4". And then, of course, to make the week worse we suffered a PHPocalpyse... Plus, Chuck Randolph of 360 Privacy explains how the internet has made it scarily easy to put company executives and public officials in danger. All this and more in episode 490 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest James Ball.

recent_posts.title: Popcorn Time’s forgotten updater left millions of devices exposed to hijacking
recent_posts.text: The update process for an abandoned streaming app could let attackers take over PCs. If you ever used Popcorn Time, check your devices. You may have forgotten about Popcorn Time. Unfortunately, its updater didn’t forget about your device. Security researchers have intervened to disable an abandoned update mechanism in Time4Popcorn, a version of the once-popular streaming app. If left running in the background, the updater could have allowed attackers to take control of Windows and Mac computers, even if their owners hadn’t opened the app in years. Eye Security estimates that the vulnerable updater was present on millions of devices worldwide, including 2.5–3 million Windows computers and around 250,000–350,000 Macs. Popcorn Time made watching movies and TV shows through BitTorrent look more like browsing Netflix. Rather than making users find torrent files and open them in a separate client, it wrapped the process in a familiar streaming-style interface. Amid concerns about copyright infringement and its possible consequences, the original developers abandoned it shortly after its launch in 2014. Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. recent_posts.title: Malicious Firefox extensions impersonate popular crypto wallets
recent_posts.text: Fake Firefox extensions posing as Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget targeted users to steal crypto wallet recovery phrases and private keys. Socket’s threat researchers found three malicious Firefox extensions that impersonated the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets. Once installed, the malicious extensions stole recovery phrases and private keys, which would provide the attacker with full control of a wallet. A crypto wallet is an app, browser extension, or physical device that lets you manage cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin. Despite its name, it doesn’t actually hold your coins. Those are recorded on a blockchain , a shared digital record of transactions. Instead, the wallet manages the secret digital keys that let you access and spend them. When you create a wallet, you may be given a recovery phrase: a list of words you can use to restore access. Write it down and store it offline. It’s a backup of your keys, not just an ordinary password. Anyone who gets hold of it can take control of your funds, which is why fake wallet extensions try to steal it. recent_posts.text: We explain how to download and read ebooks safely, whether a device can be infected through an ebook, and why pirate libraries and free-book sites are dangerous. Contrary to a common misconception, people haven’t stopped enjoying books in the digital age. The truth is that for a while now, reading on paper hasn’t been the only way to enjoy written word. At first glance, what cybersecurity risks could there possibly be? Unfortunately, as readers are a huge audience and demand for ebooks is high, cybercriminals are bound to try to cash in. We spoke with Andrey Sidenko, Head of Child Online Safety at Kaspersky, to learn how criminals exploit interest in ebooks and what to look out for so you don’t become a victim. Malware instead of a book Most often, scammers target computer and smartphone users who try to download an ebook from a pirate site. For example, our experts recently discovered a miner spreading this way: it was tapping the processing power of infected computers to generate various cryptocurrency tokens. The Department of Justice sued Alaska last month, arguing that an alleged scheme by Peltola to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, an independent candidate who shares a name with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, would confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign, the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee and civic groups including the League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause all filed motions to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the federal government lacks standing and constitutional authority to weigh in on Alaska’s elections. recent_posts.title: Five election scams to watch out for
recent_posts.text: Election messages can ask you to register, donate, take a survey, or buy merchandise. Here’s how to check before you click or pay. Elections give scammers plenty to work with: urgent deadlines, familiar faces, passionate supporters, and messages asking people to take action. Some want you to “fix” your voter registration. Others want a donation, an answer to a survey, or payment for merchandise supposedly endorsed by your favorite politician. The details change, but the objective stays the same: get your money, your personal information , or both. Here are five election-themed scams to watch out for. Scam 1. “We’ll help you vote” Not every election-themed lure starts with a threat. Some offer to make voting easier. “Get your ballot on autopilot,” reads one text message we reviewed. It encourages recipients to join a permanent absentee list so their ballots arrive at home for every election, adding the reassuring words: “Verified. Tracked. Counted.” A voting-assistance text message reviewed by Scam Guard The message is a scam, though it borrows the language of a real Minnesota voting service. recent_posts.title: Applying Security by Design and Cyber Immunity principles to protect AI systems | Kaspersky official blog
recent_posts.text: How organizations can use the basic principles of secure system design to reduce the risks of deploying AI agents: a guide for AI system architects and security teams. AI systems are much harder to protect than traditional IT — whether from operator mistakes, malicious interference, or just plain unstable behavior. There are two main reasons for this. First, AI outputs are probabilistic , so the same prompt can give different answers each time you run it. Second, today’s LLMs can’t reliably tell commands apart from data . Despite the demonstrated security issues of AI systems that we’ve covered many times, it’s impossible to ignore the potential economic payoff of adopting them. That’s why many companies are moving beyond simple AI assistants to AI agents. These agents carry out tasks on their own and have direct access to the same tools as humans — from reading databases to changing settings in production processes. Our experts, in their new study , examine how to clearly define and minimize the resulting risks to keep potential problems to a minimum. recent_posts.title: Russia Is Tightening Internet Controls, Leading to Operational Risks
recent_posts.text: Explore Russia's escalating internet restrictions, VPN bans, and outages, and understand the growing operational and surveillance risks for organizations. Executive Summary Since mid-2025, the Kremlin has intensified restrictions on digital communications and infrastructure, very likely to suppress the organization of domestic political dissent and conduct digital surveillance within Russia. Increasingly strict measures targeting virtual private networks (VPNs), state-managed internet shutdowns, limitations on civilian communications platforms, and monitoring of domestic and foreign entities very likely represent an escalation from the approaches to censorship and surveillance pursued prior to 2024. However, despite intensifying internet restrictions, technical and political limitations will likely prevent the Kremlin from achieving its long-held objective of a fully “sovereign internet” in the near term. The most likely scenario is that Moscow exerts extensive censorship and monitoring of online activity with increasingly strict –– though not absolute –– controls on circumvention and anonymizing tools.
